blocks.text: Chromosomal mutations are large-scale changes in the position of genes or in the structure or number of chromosomes. They are usually spontaneous.

Chromosomal rearrangements are physical changes such as deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations, usually caused by breaks in the DNA double helix at two places. In a translocation a segment of one chromosome becomes part of another; in an inversion the orientation of part of a chromosome is reversed.

blocks.alt: Four panels of banded chromosomes, each Before and After. Deletion: a boxed blue segment is lost. Duplication: the boxed blue segment appears twice. Translocation: the boxed ends of chromosome 4 and chromosome 20 swap places. Inversion: a segment between two breaks is turned round, so its coloured bands are in reverse order. Every chromosome keeps its centromere.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.24: Chromosomal rearrangements (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.24).

blocks.text: Insertional inactivation: many small pieces of DNA, transposons or jumping genes, can move from one place in the genome to another, choosing new locations at random. Some insert into genes and inactivate them; this is common in nature, and many human genetic disorders result from it. For example, a human transposon inserted into the clotting factor IX gene on the X chromosome places a stop codon in the middle of the gene and causes X-linked haemophilia.

Occasionally chromosomes fail to separate properly in meiosis, so a gamete gains or loses a chromosome. This is non-disjunction; if such a gamete forms a zygote the individual may have severe abnormalities. It can affect autosomes or sex chromosomes.

blocks.title: Tidbit: the mother's age
blocks.text: Non-disjunction is much more likely to build up over time in eggs than in sperm, because all of a woman's future eggs have reached prophase I by the time she is born, so they are as old as she is, while men make new sperm daily. The mother's age therefore matters more than the father's.

The total chromosome number is 47 (2n+1). It was first described in 1866 by J. Langdon Down and affects about 1 in every 750 children. It is caused by non-disjunction of autosome pair 21, which can happen when an egg forms: the pair fails to separate, giving an egg with 24 chromosomes, and fertilization by a normal sperm gives a child, male or female, with trisomy 21. Symptoms include mental impairment, stunted growth, extra skin on the back of the neck, flat facial features, a small head, short neck and limbs, upward-slanting eyes, small ears, poor muscle tone, a protruding tongue and heart defects. Males are usually sterile and females have lower fertility. Good management, with screening for common problems, medical treatment, a good family environment and special education, improves quality of life.

blocks.alt: A human karyotype: chromosome pairs 1 to 22 in three rows, aligned at their centromeres, with three copies of chromosome 21 circled in red; the sex chromosomes are shown as X and Y, or X and X.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.25: Karyotype of Down syndrome (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.25).

blocks.text: If the X chromosomes fail to separate in the mother, an egg may get both X chromosomes (XX) or none (O). An XX egg fertilized by a Y sperm gives XXY, with 47 chromosomes (44 + XXY); non-disjunction in the father can also give an XY sperm, which with a normal X egg gives XXY. This is Klinefelter syndrome, named after the American physician Harry Klinefelter, who described it in 1942. Affected boys grow into sterile males with some female characteristics (less body hair, breast growth), small testes, long legs, a short trunk, shoulders about as wide as the hips and a less deep voice. Treatment includes testosterone from puberty, surgical removal of breast tissue, and behavioural therapy for language, school and social difficulties.

blocks.alt: A human karyotype: chromosome pairs 1 to 22 in three rows, aligned at their centromeres, and the sex chromosomes X, X and Y circled in red, 47 chromosomes in all.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.26: Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.26).

blocks.title: Tidbit: triple X
blocks.text: An XX egg fertilized by an X sperm gives a girl with 47 chromosomes and XXX, triple X syndrome. Such females may have learning disabilities, tall stature and wide-spaced eyes; they are fertile and reach puberty at the normal age.

An O egg with a Y sperm gives an OY zygote, which does not develop, because humans cannot survive without the genes on the X chromosome. An O egg with an X sperm, or an O sperm with an X egg, gives a girl with 45 chromosomes, XO (2n-1 or 44 + XO), a monosomy of the sex chromosomes: Turner syndrome, first described by the American endocrinologist Henry Turner in 1938. Features include short stature, a webbed neck, immature sex organs and infertility, low mental abilities, and a small chin and jaw. It is linked with liver and kidney problems, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure. It occurs roughly once in every 2500 female births. Growth hormone started early in childhood improves growth, and estrogen replacement brings on secondary sexual characteristics.

blocks.alt: Left, nondisjunction during egg formation: an XX cell gives an O egg and an XX egg; fusion with normal X or Y sperm gives XO (female, Turner syndrome), OY (inviable), XXY (male, Klinefelter syndrome) and XXX (female, XXX syndrome). Right, nondisjunction during sperm formation: an XY cell gives O and XY sperm; fusion with normal X eggs gives XO (female, Turner syndrome) and XXY (male, Klinefelter syndrome).
blocks.caption: Figure 19.27: Nondisjunction of sex chromosomes (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.27).

blocks.title: Tidbit: extra or missing autosomes
blocks.text: A zygote missing an autosome cannot complete development, and most with an extra autosome do not survive. However, chromosomes 13, 15, 18, 21 and 22 can be present in three copies and the individual can survive for a time. An extra 13, 15 or 18 causes severe defects and death within a few months; individuals with an extra 21 or 22 usually survive to adulthood, with delayed skeletal maturation, short stature, poor muscle tone and affected mental development.
